newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers nervously watch tobacco negotiations.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers nervously watch tobacco negotiations.

text.p: Congressional friends and foes of the tobacco industry are watching the negotiations between states and cigarette makers warily, because Congress would have to vote on any legislation to ratify a settlement.

Smoking opponents, whose power waned when Republicans took control of Congress in 1994, are actively trying to influence the negotiations by warning they would try to block any deal giving cigarette makers broad immunity from future lawsuits.
They are also mulling new restrictions on tobacco that go far beyond the current scope of the talks, arguing that with the industry on the ropes, Congress should exact tough concessions.

Asked if anti-smoking lawmakers were trying to direct the course of negotiations, Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., said, "Yes. And it's not unreasonable if this agreement is ultimately to be ratified by Congress."

Tobacco's long-time friends have been relatively quiet as they try to assess the chances of a settlement and the impact of a recent North Carolina court ruling paving the way for the government to regulate nicotine as a drug.

Some lawmakers who fought federal controls on tobacco for years are now trying to adjust to a world where industry appears willing to embrace some restrictions. They want to know what a settlement could mean for tobacco farmers they represent.

"If the tobacco companies make the decision that they think they can do this ... that's a judgment they have to make," said Kentucky Republican Representative Ed Whitfield, who met with industry officials on Capitol Hill this week.
"If there's going to be some agreement you have to take (farmers) into consideration, at least the possibility they have their (crop) allotments bought out," he said.

Away from Congress, 29 state attorneys general continue talks with cigarette makers. Industry officials hope to settle state lawsuits seeking to make them pay the Medicaid costs of treating smoking-related illness.

The two sides have talked about a plan under which tobacco firms would reportedly provide up to $300 billion in compensation over 25 years and accept a host of new federal restrictions. In return, the industry initially sought broad immunity from future lawsuits.
States appear to be taking a harder line on immunity after the North Carolina ruling, but whether there ultimately will be a deal is anyone's guess.
Lawmakers may be watching closely, but they do not appear eager to grapple with a settlement. Opponents are leery of the industry and supporters fear a messy legislative battle.

"I'm sure Congress doesn't want to deal with this. Their history in the past on settlements or other dealings with tobacco has not been great. Tobacco has always come out a winner," said Josh Cooper of the American Lung Association.
One factor sure to drive any debate is money, and lots of it.

The tobacco industry gave $9.9 million to Washington politicians during 1995-1996, according to the public interest group Common Cause. The majority of tobacco contributions went to Republicans. For instance, Philip Morris gave more than $3 million in 1995-1996, with $2.5 million directed to Republicans, according to the Centre for Responsive Politics.

On the other side is the Association of Trial Lawyers of America, which opposes any settlement that would preclude future lawsuits. It gives mainly to Democrats, although its war chest is a quarter of the size of the tobacco industry's.

The industry may have lost some court battles, but it has key supporters in Congress, such as House Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican, and Senate Assistant Democratic Leader Wendell Ford of Kentucky.

In recent weeks, tobacco opponents have pushed legislation to clamp down on the industry. Under debate are bills to triple the federal cigarette tax to pay for childrens' health care, phase out crop insurance for tobacco farmers and boost federal regulation of tobacco.

Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Edward Kennedy has suggested attaching new restrictions to any deal, such as one that would allow opponents to go after the profits of non-tobacco subsidiaries of cigarette makers.
